candidate.answerReason: Twice Susie's purchase costs the same as Calvin's. Canceling their common items shows that 6 muffins cost as much as 10 bananas, giving a price ratio of 5/3.

methods.label: Cancel common items from equal-cost purchases
methods.explanation:
Two copies of Susie's purchase would contain 8 muffins and 6 bananas. Their cost equals Calvin's spending, because Calvin spends twice as much as Susie.

Thus 8 muffins and 6 bananas cost the same as 2 muffins and 16 bananas. Subtract the cost of 2 muffins and 6 bananas from both purchases. This leaves 6 muffins costing the same as 10 bananas.

Using the positive price of a banana as one unit of cost, one muffin therefore costs
\[
\frac{10}{6}=\frac53
\]
units. A muffin is \(\boxed{\frac53}\) times as expensive as a banana, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: Comparing equal-cost groups and canceling common costs gives an arithmetic ratio solution without a system of equations.

candidate.annotationRationale: The route-neutral target is the ratio of the two unit prices. The written method uses total-cost relationships and subtraction of a common component to obtain that ratio. Equation-modeling and parenthesis-solving nodes are unnecessary for this arithmetic route.
